items.title: Lunette of Saint Anna, the Virgin and 2 Monks
items.description:
A Ceramic Lunette, which is rendered in 8 parts. The central image shows the Madonna and child. Behind Mary, with a hand on her shoulders is St. Anne; they are positioned to appear as if Mary is Sitting on Anne's lap with the infant Christ subsequently sitting in hers. Two Male saints kneel, one on each side, with their heads bowed toward the infant Christ. The three saints are haloed, thought the Virgin and Child are not, presumably because the are suspended too far forward in relief and would block the other figures. Around the top of the arch a Mask is presented at the crown of the arch, sculpted greenery and fruits then fall down either side of the arch.
Saint Anne is identified in her hagiography as the mother of the Virgin Mary. This explains her positioning with this pointedly young-looking depiction of the Virgin. Mary wears blue, so she stands out completely against the white glaze finish of her mother, the other two saints, and the Baby in her lap. The three older saints in turn stand out against the blue background, with Saint Anne acting as a sort of border around the Virgin.
The male saint on the right side of the image (when viewing) is St. Dominic. He holds a cross, Lilies and a book (there is also a scull nestled in the crook of his arm, though this is less typical of his attributes). He is dressed in robes and has his hair cut into a tonsure but is clean shaven.
The Second male saint, on the left side, is St. Augustine of Hippo. He holds a book against his knee. The symbol of a book is very common among saints, but is an attribute of Augustine. In his other hand he holds what appears to be a flaming heart, which would be a more identifiable symbols of Augustine.

items.title: Roman Vestal
items.description:
A bust of a Roman Vestal. She is depicted from the chest up, and her head is hooded with thin cloth that drapes to her shoulders, joining the fabric of her dress or tunic. Her hair is visible laying flat and unbound beneath the cloak, though her bangs are styled back away from her face. Her features are soft and she casts her eyes downward.
The Vestals (Also called Vestal Virgins), were a group of priestesses of the Roman goddess Vesta. Vesta is goddess of the hearth, home and family, more often represented herself as a sacred flame than in human form (Her Greek equivalent is Hestia). The Vestals who oversaw her sacred temples were selected before puberty and took vows to the goddess, which lasted 30 years. During this period they were expected to stay virgins, and breaking their vow of chastity was met with either burning or entombment. In addition to the vows of Chastity, Vestals pledged their service to the goddess, learning and performing rites which were thought to maintain the Roman State.
In exchange they were the only ones allowed to enter the temples of Vesta, which they did to maintain the sacred fire in her hearth, and they were granted privileges above those of all other women in the empire, including those women in the royal family. Rights of the Vestals included: The ability to use a carpentum, a two-wheeled horse drawn carriage not dissimilar to those ridden by triumphant generals in processions; right away, with the impeding a Vestal's passing being punishable by death; access to and ring-side seating at public games including gladiatorial fights and plays.
Additionally a Vesta could pardon any condemned person who was en route to execution, simply by touching them, so long as the meeting had not been pre-arranged.

items.title: Venus of Cyrene
items.description:
A statue of a Venus, presented in the Nude standing contrapposto. She is missing her head and arms, but otherwise is very in tact. If the image was fully in tact, it would have presented a young goddess emerging from the water, Right hand lowered to cover herself, and left hand reaching to pick up the cloth; At the right hip of the Venus the image of a hydra with a fish in it's mouth is coiled on it's front with drapery hanging from the tail of the creature (presumably the dress of the Venus herself).
This image is a recreation of the Venus of Cyrene, which was excavated in 1913. The original was dated to approximately 130 A.C. and was itself a copy of the Venus Cnidia by Praxiteles, (known only through Roman copies). Praxiteles is accredited with the first depiction of a female nude in the cannon of Greek works of art.
In 2002 the Venus of Cyrene was transferred from the Minister of Cultural Heritage and Activities in Italy to the Libyan Republic in a repatriation that was surrounded in criticism. The deal was finalized in 2008 and the work was sent to a small museum with minimal security. As Libya descended into revolution in 2011, artifacts from Cyrene were targeted, located and sold on the black market or destroyed my militant groups moving through the area. The exact fate of the Venus is not known, but it was confirmed to have disappeared from the museum housing it. Sometimes referred to as the "Lost Venus" it can be viewed in the form of a plaster mold taken in the 1930s, but the fate of the original is not known.

items.title: Spring
items.description:
A terracotta statue of Spring, envisioned as a young woman. Draped in a toga, and barefoot with her hair pulled up in a bun at the top of her neck. She holds a bouquet of leaves and roses at her left hip.

Once the item is sculpted it is dried naturally for approximately 30 days before being fired for 72 hours in a kiln that reaches approximately 1,050 degrees centigrade.

items.title: Bronze Statue of Moses (after Michelangelo)
items.description:
A Bronze cast statue after Michelangelo's Moses. The statue is rendered in a very high degree of detail showing Moses with short hair, but a very long beard, which curls in tendrils down his chest and is met by the fingers of his hand. Seated on a large block, the right foot is planted in front of the body, and the left is angled back toward his side. Under his right arm two tablets (Those which presented the ten commandments) are propped, held in place on the stone. He is dressed in a sleeveless tunic, which gathers in large pleats and drapes over his lap, leaving defined, muscular arms and the lower legs and sandaled feet exposed.
The original Statue by Michelangelo was commissioned by Pole Julius II for his tomb. The commission took 40 years to complete, 1505-1545. Pope Julius died in 1513 and did not see the completion of the tomb. It is carved from marble and stands approximately 3x the size of the bronze at Krebs House.

items.title: St. Francis of Assisi
items.description:
Bronze statue depicting St. Francis of Assisi. He stands with a tall posture, though his attention is cast downward, as if he is looking at someone or something that is shorter than him. His face is kind and open, and he has a shortly cropped beard and mustache. He is dressed in the traditional Franciscan Habit of a long robe tied at the waist with a rope. St. Francis' hood is down, showing his Tonsure. Two birds have perched on him, one on the right wrist, the other in his left hand.
St. Francis is the patron of Animals, Merchants and Ecology and his Feast-Day is on February 4th. Born in Assisi in Umbria (Modern Italy), he is best known as the founder of the Franciscan monastic order. His father was a merchant, and tradition says he had an easy-going temperament and happy manner. Francis' conversion from a man of business to a man of God followed a failed attempt at the Crusades, from which he returned without seeing battle. He eventually found himself at a Church at San Damiano, where the image of Christ on the crucifix implored him to repair the Chapel.

items.title: Madonna and Child
items.description:
Stucco Bas-relief of the Madonna and Child. The image was created by Antonio Rossellino and his workshop in Ferrara. This particular image seems to sit between Rossellino's early mature style - defined by vibrant and dynamic compositions - and his later style - known for more severe and solid image productions.
It is ascribed to be part of the "Candelabra Madonnas," a group of works by Rossellino which are identified by the consistent depiction of two lighted candelabras in the background of the image. The shared prototype of the Candelabra images is a terracotta bas-relief, which is currently housed at the Victoria and Albert museum and dated between 1465 and 1470. Two sizes of exist within this group, the larger set of which almost identically match the Prototype. However, the image in the LFC collection belongs in the smaller size group, which tends to show variations from the original and between each piece.

items.title: Coronation of the Virgin (Model in Clay)
items.description:
A bozzetto, or rough clay sculpture, done as a model in prepreparation of a larger piece. In this case, the final work was probably intended to be an altarpiece. The image depicts the Virgin Mary being coronated as the Queen of Heaven.
Mary herself is pictured twice. Once in the bottom half of the image, she is depicted on earth, kneeling before a group of saints who observe her coronation. Second, in the upper half of the image, she kneels to receive the crown in Heaven.
Alongside her in the upper half of the sculpture the Holy Trinity is depicted, ready to anoint her with the crown. Jesus the son crouches on the left side of the image, indicated by the cross behind him; it seems to be supported by his left arm which is not shown in the relief. His right hand supports the crown. God the father sits on the right hand side. His right hand holds up the crown, and his left rests on a globe, probably meant to depict the world, which is supported by a cherub. The Holy Spirit is depicted above the scene as a dove, flying as a focal point at the top of the image.
The earthly scene depicts the Virgin, almost directly beneath the upper image so they are both centered, though the earthly image seems positioned slightly to the side by the forward push of the saints depicted along the left side of the image. From left to right in the front row, the Attending Saints are identified as: Saint John Nepomuk, Saint Dominic, A praying female saint (Probably Catherine of Siena, but could also be Saint Theresa). In the back row of saints who move from left to right, behind the Virgin: A male saint who holds himself upright with a cane in his left hand (Probably Francis of Paola, but could also be Antony the Abbot/Antony the Great), Saint Joachim, Saint Anne, and Saint Appolonia (holding a tooth). Saint John the Baptist stands to the right side of the Virgin with his right hand raised over her, as if he is doing the earthly anointing.

items.title: Night (After Michelangelo)
items.description:
A replica of Michelangelo's Night, carved in Alabaster. Both the original and the replica in the LFC collection are part of set, though their counterparts are not the same between the sets.
The image of Night depicts a woman lounged leaning on her left arm. The right leg is relaxed, following the shape of the arch on which she sits. Her left leg is drawn up to support the right arm, on which her head is leaned in turn. Tipped down, as if to use the arm to block the light, the figure's eyes are closed, sleeping. Her hair is drawn back, using a band to keep it away from her face, though some of it falls back over her left shoulder. The pose is serene in it's stillness.
The recreations in the LFC collection are significantly smaller than the original images, which adorn the Tomb of Giuliano de Medici. The original Night Sculpture was carved between 1526 and 1531 and is approximately 59" x 60". Likely as a result of the change in size, the replicas have been simplified, including the removal of an owl, who sits in the crook of Night's elevated leg in the original. It adorns the left side of the Sarcophagus and is accompanied on the right side by a depiction of Day - rendered as a man lounging in the opposite direction. All of the original statues were carved in Marble and are still installed in the Medici Chapel in Florence. The two figures of Night and Dawn are the only two female nudes ever depicted by Michelangelo.

items.title: Susanna
items.description:
A statue of Suzanna, as lifted from her story within the Bible. She is seated, pitched forward, and looking over her shoulder, moving to cover herself as she realizes her uninvited audience. She is draped in patterned fabrics that sit low around her waist, and her hair is held up with a scarf. Earrings are her only other adornments as she holds herself on the rockwork base, which is carved with foliage. At her feet a stream runs.
The story of Suzanna is one commonly depicted in art. Also called Suzanna and the elders, the story is told of a beautiful young woman. In the privacy of her walled garden, Suzanna bathes, but is spied by two elders of the village, both of whom covet her. Working together they try to bribe her into having sex, threatening to say she has committed adultery if she refuses. When she refuses, the elders hold to the threat and make a public accusation of adultery. It is only after the two men are cross-examined by Daniel and reveal discrepancies in their stories that Suzanna is proven innocent.
Her pedestal depicts Biblical scenes. Suzanna's story is only considered to be canonical in the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches.In these denominations the story is part of the book of Daniel. In most other denominations of Christianity, Suzanna's story is not considered cannon, but it is considered to be useful for teaching. The motif of the story is very common in artwork. Images depicting the tale date back to as early as the 9th century. It was particularly popular in the 15th and 16th centuries. When painted the image usually depicts Suzanna and the two voyeurs in a scene. When sculpted in the round, Suzanna is usually depicted alone.
In the context of Krebs House, the Suzanna statue (KR23.2.27) sits atop the White Marble Pedestal (KR23.3.10), framed by a Italian Stone Rotunda (KR23.3.11), and set as the focal point of a fountain.

items.title: 1 of 2 Italian Statues (Hebe)
items.description:
Statue of a the Greek Goddess Hebe. She stands almost at Contrapposto, but looks more poised for movement, like she is about to step forward. In her right hand she holds a jug at her hip. The left holds a smaller dish, held at chest height, either for her to drink from or for her to pass. She wears a floor-length toga, that drapes from her left shoulder, leaving the right side of her chest bare. Her hair is pulled back, away from her face leaving her eyes visible where they look forward, past the cup, presumably to the viewer.
Hebe was primarily venerated as a goddess of eternal youth and the prime of life; Secondarily some groups also worship her as a goddess of forgiveness and mercy. She was the daughter of Zeus and Hera, divine wife of Hercules and the youngest of the Pantheon. Her primary role was as the cup bearer of the gods. This is related to her dominion over eternal youth and life, which she ensured by bearing ambrosia. She is sometimes depicted as an Eagle which bears a cup in it's talon instead of as a woman.
Her Roman counterpart is Juventas.

items.title: Diana Gabis (1 of 4 goddess statues)
items.description:
A depiction of the Roman goddess Diana. She stands dressed in sandals, and a tunic-style dress with flowing sleeves, She is positioned with two ends of a cloak in hand, reaching up to her right shoulder to fasten the clasp. Her hair is short and held in place by a band as she looks off to the left.

There are several known copies of the original statue, which has been lost to time. The most famous recreation is the Diana of Gabi which is on display at the Louvre in Paris. This version was acquired in 1807, and is featured as a part of the Bourghese Collection. The statue at the Louvre is slightly larger at 165 cm high.

items.title: Diana Amazzone (2 of 4 goddess statues)
items.description:
The Roman goddess Diana depicted as an Amazon. She stands with her bow braced on her left shoulder, though not drawn, and a quiver at her hip. She wears a Toga that is draped from her right shoulder, where the arm reaches up to grasp the top of the bow. A tree stump supports her hip, and Rocky, unpaved earth is depicted under her feet. This is one of a few variations on the motif of the wounded Amazon, the wound is meant to be visible under the right breast.
Wounded Amazon Sculptures appear in a few variations, with the most significant differences being the positioning of the hands, coverage of the chiton, and the presence (or lack there of) of the bow and quiver. This statue seems to be a replica of a version on display at the Capitoline Museums in Rome. Replicas of this type are typically thought to have emerged in approximately 10 B.C. to 10 A.D., the first imperial period. The original which they copy is attributed to the Greek Sculptor Phidias (c. 480 – 430 BC), full replicas of which have not survived, thus the assorted variations. Older versions have largely lost the associated original head of the statue, the recreation at the Capitoline Museum used a reconstruction of the head of a different Amazon (potentially Diana) statue attributed to Polykleitos (5th Century BC). The statue at the Capitoline Museums was restored to add the head in 1775, and stands 197cm tall, slightly larger than the 160 cm. recreation in the Lake Forest Collection.

items.title: Venus Callipyge (3 of 4 Goddess Statues).
items.description:
A depiction of Venus, which shows her lifting a section of the Peplos so that her buttocks and legs are bare, though she appears covered from the front, with the skirts there hanging down and a short-sleeved top on the tunic remains in place. Venus herself twists gracefully, arms bringing the ends of her skirt up closer to her shoulders, and back arched so she can look over her shoulder and down toward her exposed backside, as if to admire.
The Venus in the garden at LFC is a recreation of the Venus Callipyge, which dates to the 1st or 2nd century BC (itself a recreation of a Greek Statue, which was probably executed in Bronze around 300 BC). The head was lost with the original, and has been subsequently recreated twice (The second closely following the first) in the 16th and 18th century. The 1st century "original" is currently on display at the National Archeological Museum in Napes, France.
The statue can also be called Aphrodite Kallipygos, or the Callipygian Venus. All versions of the name translate to "Venus (or Aphrodite) of the beautiful buttocks."

items.title: Madonna & Blessing Child
items.description:
Relief of the Virgin Mary and an Infant Jesus, which is attributed to the workshop of Donatello. Very likely, this work is a copy done off of either a modello or a finished relief which has been lost to time. The original would have been done by the master himself. The relief is likely from the period of 1445-1455, during the artist's time running his work shop out of Florence.
The image depicts the Virgin Mary, wearing red and draped with blue, holding the infant Jesus loosely, more like she is supporting an infant learning to walk, than actually holding him. The Christ Child himself stands and moves forward, his right foot positioned as if he is stepping off from the edge of the frame. His right arm is raised to give a blessing, as if there is someone standing just to the side of the image. He is wrapped in white and red, and haloed. The Virgin and child, as well as the two seraphims and angels behind them are all haloed with large, bright gold disks that are decoratively pitted to match the bordering the image. The composition is rendered in "a stiacciato" ("flattened relief"), which maintains the volume and depth of the relief while focusing on the pictorial qualities of the composition.
This image is typical to the Marin Typology, which have been largely attributed to Donatello's Florentine workshop. They are very similar in their depiction of the Virgin and Child, and identifiable by the positioning of the child in the position seen here, as if he is ready to move and bless. Approximately 10 of these images are currently known, though the image in the LFC collection sticks out among them due to the difference in ornamentation. The use of gold, and the depiction of Haloes as full, wide, ornamented disks rather than foreshortening them as seen in the rest of the images is particular to this piece. This additional ornamentation seems to suggest that the work was designed as a devotional object in it's own right, rather than a smaller component part of a larger altar as the other Marin reliefs are.

items.title: Plaster Relief Madonna & Child
items.description:
A plaster relief showing the Madonna and Child. The Child is nestled in a bed of earth or straw, and the Virgin kneels above him. She looks down lovingly upon her child with her hands steepled in front of her in adoration. Two angels are depicted in the blue field of the sky behind them and two hands lower a crown to the Virgin's head.A bush of lilies grows behind the infant's head.
The Plaster relief shows a great deal of dimension, sitting far enough forward that it almost counts as high relief, though the figures are attached across the whole of the back. A border at the bottom shows three cherubs with laurels strung between them.
The relief in the collection is a modern rendition of a 15th century work in the style of Andrea Della Robbia. The Della Robbia style is identified by the bright colored glazes (Traditionally applied over terra cotta so that the color soaked in to the clay), mostly in combinations of blues and whites. This image is rendered in plaster instead of terracotta but holds the typical colors of the style which the piece is trying to emulate. Della Robbia's shop made several variations on the image of the mother and child, but the one most closely represented in the LFC recreation is "Adoration of the Child" made around 1470, and currently on display at the Museo Nazionale del Bargello, Florence

items.title: Lunette of Saint Anna, the Virgin and 2 Monks
items.description:
A Ceramic Lunette, which is rendered in 8 parts. The central image shows the Madonna and child. Behind Mary, with a hand on her shoulders is St. Anne; they are positioned to appear as if Mary is Sitting on Anne's lap with the infant Christ subsequently sitting in hers. Two Male saints kneel, one on each side, with their heads bowed toward the infant Christ. The three saints are haloed, thought the Virgin and Child are not, presumably because the are suspended too far forward in relief and would block the other figures. Around the top of the arch a Mask is presented at the crown of the arch, sculpted greenery and fruits then fall down either side of the arch.
Saint Anne is identified in her hagiography as the mother of the Virgin Mary. This explains her positioning with this pointedly young-looking depiction of the Virgin. Mary wears blue, so she stands out completely against the white glaze finish of her mother, the other two saints, and the Baby in her lap. The three older saints in turn stand out against the blue background, with Saint Anne acting as a sort of border around the Virgin.
The male saint on the right side of the image (when viewing) is St. Dominic. He holds a cross, Lilies and a book (there is also a scull nestled in the crook of his arm, though this is less typical of his attributes). He is dressed in robes and has his hair cut into a tonsure but is clean shaven.
The Second male saint, on the left side, is St. Augustine of Hippo. He holds a book against his knee. The symbol of a book is very common among saints, but is an attribute of Augustine. In his other hand he holds what appears to be a flaming heart, which would be a more identifiable symbols of Augustine.

items.title: Roman Vestal
items.description:
A bust of a Roman Vestal. She is depicted from the chest up, and her head is hooded with thin cloth that drapes to her shoulders, joining the fabric of her dress or tunic. Her hair is visible laying flat and unbound beneath the cloak, though her bangs are styled back away from her face. Her features are soft and she casts her eyes downward.
The Vestals (Also called Vestal Virgins), were a group of priestesses of the Roman goddess Vesta. Vesta is goddess of the hearth, home and family, more often represented herself as a sacred flame than in human form (Her Greek equivalent is Hestia). The Vestals who oversaw her sacred temples were selected before puberty and took vows to the goddess, which lasted 30 years. During this period they were expected to stay virgins, and breaking their vow of chastity was met with either burning or entombment. In addition to the vows of Chastity, Vestals pledged their service to the goddess, learning and performing rites which were thought to maintain the Roman State.
In exchange they were the only ones allowed to enter the temples of Vesta, which they did to maintain the sacred fire in her hearth, and they were granted privileges above those of all other women in the empire, including those women in the royal family. Rights of the Vestals included: The ability to use a carpentum, a two-wheeled horse drawn carriage not dissimilar to those ridden by triumphant generals in processions; right away, with the impeding a Vestal's passing being punishable by death; access to and ring-side seating at public games including gladiatorial fights and plays.
Additionally a Vesta could pardon any condemned person who was en route to execution, simply by touching them, so long as the meeting had not been pre-arranged.

items.title: Venus of Cyrene
items.description:
A statue of a Venus, presented in the Nude standing contrapposto. She is missing her head and arms, but otherwise is very in tact. If the image was fully in tact, it would have presented a young goddess emerging from the water, Right hand lowered to cover herself, and left hand reaching to pick up the cloth; At the right hip of the Venus the image of a hydra with a fish in it's mouth is coiled on it's front with drapery hanging from the tail of the creature (presumably the dress of the Venus herself).
This image is a recreation of the Venus of Cyrene, which was excavated in 1913. The original was dated to approximately 130 A.C. and was itself a copy of the Venus Cnidia by Praxiteles, (known only through Roman copies). Praxiteles is accredited with the first depiction of a female nude in the cannon of Greek works of art.
In 2002 the Venus of Cyrene was transferred from the Minister of Cultural Heritage and Activities in Italy to the Libyan Republic in a repatriation that was surrounded in criticism. The deal was finalized in 2008 and the work was sent to a small museum with minimal security. As Libya descended into revolution in 2011, artifacts from Cyrene were targeted, located and sold on the black market or destroyed my militant groups moving through the area. The exact fate of the Venus is not known, but it was confirmed to have disappeared from the museum housing it. Sometimes referred to as the "Lost Venus" it can be viewed in the form of a plaster mold taken in the 1930s, but the fate of the original is not known.

items.title: Venus Callipyge
items.description:
A modern replica of the Venus Callipyge, rendered in a much smaller scale.
THe Roman Goddess Venus is shown lifting a section of the Peplos so that her buttocks and legs are bare, though she appears covered from the front, with the skirts there hanging down and a short-sleeved top on the tunic remains in place. Venus herself twists gracefully - arms bringing the ends of her skirt up closer to her shoulders - and back, arched so she can look over her shoulder and down toward her exposed backside, as if to admire.
This is a recreation of the Venus Callipyge, which dates to the 1st or 2nd century BC (itself a recreation of a Greek Statue, which was probably executed in Bronze around 300 BC). The head was lost with the original, and has been subsequently recreated twice (The second closely following the first) in the 16th and 18th century. The 1st century "original" is currently on display at the National Archeological Museum in Napes, France.
The statue can also be called Aphrodite Kallipygos, or the Callipygian Venus. All versions of the name translate to "Venus (or Aphtrodite) of the beautiful buttocks."

items.title: St. John the Evangelist
items.description:
St. John the Evangelist is rendered in low relief bronze. He can be identified by the item held in his left hand: A dragon in a chalice. The symbol originates from a story of St. John wherein he was presented a cup of poisoned wine. When he drank from the chalice he was unharmed. A chalice acts as one of his attributes, alongside the Eagle and Scrolls. To signify the danger of the poison within, the chalice is often shown with a dragon or serpent rising from the mouth.
In this image St. John points to the chalice, aware but unafraid of the danger. He stands in an archway with his body turned to the right, the same direction which he looks. Clean shaven, but with long hair, he is dressed in a simple long sleeved robe that drapes at the shoulders.

items.title: Italian Relief: Martyrdom of St. Vitalis
items.description:
A relief rendered from Terracotta and framed. The image depicts the martyrdom of St. Vitalis, who was sentenced to death after being outed as a Christian upon rendering encouragement and proper burial to Ursicinus of Ravenna.
The Composition shows the saint at approximately the center of the image, falling headfirst into a pit. Though he is not yet underground, the image has a claustrophobic feel with a crowd surrounding him, prepared to throw earth and stones to burry him alive. The figure rendered in the foreground on the right side is rendered in the highest relief where he stands at the edge of the pit. Across the back of the image several layers of onlookers, rendered in fading degrees of detail imply a crowd pushing in on the scene. Down the left side a woman hold onto her children, who recoil from the scene. A dog is depicted in the lower right corner next to a shovel. At the top of the image a putti descends from heaven holding palm leaves and a crown.
The image in LFC's collection is a copy of a larger painting by Frederico Barocci, completed in 1503. The original oil painting measures 119" x 105.5" and is rendered in full color.

items.title: Madonna with Angels
items.description:
A relief sculpture cast from paster. It depicts the Virgin Mary, standing straight backed and looking out over the viewer with a calm sort of serenity on her face. Supported on her right arm, the infant Christ is settled, looking in the same direction with a similar expression. He left hand holds his right over both of their hearts and his free hand loops over her shoulder to hold on. Surrounding them are five angels, all of whom are depicted young and appear looking on the Madonna and Child with open wonder on their faces.
The image is a (probably Modern) reproduction of a work originally carved from Marble. The original sculptor, Agostino di Duccio (1418 – c. 1481), was active in Prato alongside Donatello and Michelozzo. Both of the other artists' influence can be seen in his work. The Madonna with Angels was worked on between the years of 1463 and 1470. It is displayed in the Bargello in Florence, Italy. The recreation seems to be on the same scale.

items.title: Hebe
items.description:
A marble statue of a the Greek Goddess Hebe. She was primarily venerated as a goddess of eternal youth and the prime of life; Secondarily some groups also worship her as a goddess of forgiveness and mercy. She was the daughter of Zeus and Hera, divine wife of Hercules and the youngest of the Pantheon.
Her primary role was as the cup bearer of the gods. This is related to her dominion over eternal youth and life, which she ensured by bearing ambrosia. She is sometimes depicted as an Eagle which bears a cup in it's talon instead of as a woman.
Her Roman counterpart is Juventas.

items.title: Diana as a Wounded Amazon
items.description:
19th century Marble statue identified as Diana. Her posing is archetypal to representations of the Mattei Wounded Amazon. Many artists depicted the subject matter of Amazons in the Greek and Roman worlds, however this pose - Contrapposto with the right arm raised above the head stands out as it's own archetype. This Amazon has been wounded, and raises her arm over her head to relieve the pain from her side. She is dressed in a Chiton that falls from her right shoulder, belts at the waist, then falls to knee length. At her feet a roman helmet sits discarded. Her leg is supported by a log with a banner resting against it.
The Mattei sub archetype is identified by the bow grasped in her hands and the quiver in her side. The surviving original Mattei Amazon was discovered in 1770 and dated to the Augustinian error. Though it is the oldest surviving sculpture, the Roman Marble is a copy off of a 5th century B.C. attributed to Phidias. It is named after the Mattei family who first owned it, but is now on display at the Pio-Clementine Museum in the Vatican.

items.title: Venus with the Apple
items.description:
Bronze sculpture of Venus. She stands Contrapposto, with her left arm reaching down to place her clothing onto a stump of a tree. She looks to the object held in her left hand, an apple. Left nude, she stands unabashed, with her hair drawn up into a bun.
The image depicts Venus after winning a Golden Apple from Paris. According to the legend, all of the gods except Eris, the Goddess of Strife had been invited to a party. In revenge fore being excluded, Eris tossed a golden apple into the event, the fruit was engraved to say "To the fairest goddess." A competition then ensued between Hera, Athena and Venus. After several gods passed on the dubious honor, Paris, a young Trojan prince was elected to declare a winner. He presented the apple to Venus, declaring her the fairest. The story continues that to show her gratitude Venus promised Paris the most beautiful woman on earth, Helen of Troy, whose subsequent kidnapping sparked the Trojan War.
This sculpture seems to be a copy off of an original Marble by Bertel Thorvaldsen, who created several versions of the sculpture with the earliest starting around 1813 or 1815.

items.title: Lamb of God
items.description:
A Tabernacle door that has a sculptural relief depicted on the front. The relief shows the lamb of god, haloed where it lays, holding a banner hooked in its left leg and supported against it's shoulder. The lamb lays on a book adorned with 7 seals - reminiscent of imagery from the Book of Revelations. A group of people are depicted beneath the book. The key hole to the tabernacle is visible in the front of the door beside the lamp. Removed from the rest of the item the locking mechanism is also gone.
The Lamb of God is a common symbol in Christian art. Sometimes depicting Christ, sometimes meant as it's own character from Revelations. The Lamb is a complicated symbol, simultaneously representing both suffering and triumph simultaneously. In Christ this is reflective of his crucifixion and resurrection. In the book of Revelations there are 29 references go a lamb "slain but standing." One of these lambs is the only one deemed worthy to receive the judgment scroll directly from god. The scroll (or book) contains the names of those who will be saved, perhaps represented in the figures beneath the book in the Lake Forest College collection object. The lamb is the one to break the seals. Later in Revelations another lamb is likened to the "Seven Spirits of God." What exactly these seven spirits are is currently debated but interpretations include seven distinct aspects which make up the Lord, seven distinct spiritual beings who comprise a separate class from the angels, or a representation of perfection.
The back of the Tabernacle door is gilt or otherwise covered with gold. Into this a very low relief image of a pyramid with an eye (perhaps meant to represent the eye of providence, thought the lower segment of the pyramid is not present), set against clouds and surrounded in rays of light.

items.title: Tang Horse With Rider
items.description:
A Sculpture of a horse and rider dated to the mid Tang Dynasty in China. The horse is rendered straight legged and symmetrical with ears forward and head relaxed. Sculpted from red clay connected to a flat rectangular base. It is draped in a blanket and saddle. No bridle or reins are sculpted, though remaining pigment shows these items painted on. The Horse was painted white, though much of this pigment has faded with time. It's eyes remain brightly colored red and black.
The Rider is dressed in robes and a tall square hat with sides that cover the ears. He looks more like an official than a solder and has his hands positioned in front of his stomach, as if he is holding reigns. His face is painted to depict a man with a long thin mustache and a relaxed expression. His clothing was originally painted red, how much of the pigment has faded with time. Colors were painted, not glazed.
The sculpture likely originates from the Shaanxi Province in Xian. The underside is hollow, showing that it was likely fired at least once during it's construction.

items.title: Burmese Buddha on an Elephant
items.description:
A depiction of the Buddha, who is seated on an elephant. He is nestled in the deep saddle strapped to the elephant's back, and holds something - perhaps some kind of bird - in his lap. The Buddha is presented wearing a wide collar that covers the shoulders and gauntleted gloves, with his hair arranged into the Ushnisha styling of curls atop his head. His features are carved to depict him smiling. The elephant is straight-legged with a symmetrical posture and the trunk touching the ground of the base it stands on. It wears a shaffron that covers the brow and most of the face between the eyes, as well as blankets or other draperies. These ornaments for the elephant are rendered in some detail with textured patterns depicted across the whole of the fabric. The blanket and saddle are secured with a strap across the elephant's chest. The whole statue is carved from wood and was painted over with a combination of red, black and gold paint (Or covered in gold gilt over the paint layer, which shows through). The tusks of the elephant are probably ivory, which have been affixed into the statue separately and left unpainted.
On the back of the statue the Elephant has a door cut that pulls out to reveal a hollow in the torso. There is nothing inside of the hollow, and it is unclear what the purpose of the sculpture was in it's original use (perhaps it is meant to be a reliquary?).

items.title: Chinese Rider on Horse
items.description:
Sculpted from Clay, the sculpture depicts a rider on horseback. The horse is depicted with somewhat simplified feathers including very short pointed ears and a broad flat nose. The riding tack is fully sculpted with a bridle with a spiked notch atop the nose, and harnessing straps for the saddle across the chest. The saddle itself is obscured by the riders flowing pants, but behind him the end of a saddle blanket and tasseled straps are fully sculpted. The mane is swept down the right side of the neck and the tail is sculpted so it follows the line of the left leg. The posture of the horse is straight-legged and symmetrical. The rider is slim and sits straight on it's back. He is dressed in long sleeves and a rounded hat with a wide brim. His left hand is held in front of him, curled as if holding something, though it does not survive with the sculpture. The left elbow braced with the right hand, which crosses the chest. His features depict a man with slightly chubby cheeks looking forward. The horses tack and the riders closed are glazed with a bluish pigment, but the horse's body and the man's face and hands seem to be bare reddish clay.
The Figure does not seem to be hollowed so the statue may not have been fired for finishing.

items.title: Bust of a Woman (Maybe Juno)
items.description: A marble bust of a woman who might be Juno. The sculpture is likely based on a 2nd century Roman sculpture, which does depict the roman goddess, though the iconography of the busts not specific enough to say for suer and it is not a 1 for 1 copy or expansion on the ancient sculpture. The woman is presented with strong features and a neutral expression. Her hair is pulled back from her face in the front and pinned so that hair from the back drapes forward to rest over her shoulders. A simple diadem adorns her hair. The hair is very reminiscent of the early sculptures of Juno, but notably if this sculpture is based on the second century bust, it has been added to. The original bust was once part of a colossal sculpture, but survives today broken from the base of the neck. The bust in the Krebs Collection is presented from the chest up, with the shoulders and upper torso draped in fabric which falls from the top of the shoulder.

items.title: Head of King Tut
items.description:
Carved from Granite, but bust depicts King Tut. He is shown with the same features as are presented on his golden funerary mask: eyes gazing forward, slim nose and a downturned mouth. His ears are also shown to be pierced, and the postiche (False beard) is affixed to his chin, with a line in the granite depicting where the accessory meets the skin on his cheek.
The Nemes Headdress is rendered in detail with the banded lines of color present in life depicted as details of raised carving. However, the Granite sculpture seems to have been broken, as the head of the cobra and vulture present on the funerary mask are not present on the Granite miniature. The break is clean enough that it is possible this omission was a purposeful result of the scale; The body of the cobra is present though, so this seems unlikely considering the rest of the detail work present on the sculpture.
King Tut is not posed in the sculpture as he is in his depiction on his sarcophagus, instead of being crossed over his chest, the arms lay against his side, down to where the sculpture cuts off above the elbow. he seems to be shirtless, though a collar is carved into the base of the neck and collar. A cartouche is carved into each shoulder. Tutankhamen had two distinct cartouche, however the ones on the sculpture are rendered too small with too little detail to be legible as any specific cartouche, let alone those specific to the boy king.

items.title: Crest with Medici Arms
items.description:
A ceramic crest which shows the Coat of Arms of the Medici family surrounded by a backdrop of scrolling.
The crest itself has a reddish orange field that is somewhat unusual for the typical variants of the crest. The backdrop is more typically yellow,or another light color closer to the scrolling used on the backdrop of this piece. This would likely be to make the five reddish-orange balls sick out form the backdrop. A sixth ball, painted blue with three Fleur de Lis imprinted on the surface in gold.
Variations on the Medici crest have been used over the course of the family's history, including variations used for specific members rather than the family as a whole. The exact symbolism of the Medici crest is up for debate with three core theories. The first theory is the legendary origin of the crest, which traces the Medici line back to a knight of Charlemagne by the name of Averardo. The legend claims that Averardo defeated the giant, Mugello and was awarded the shield with six dents in it as a trophy. the dents were eventually represented by the balls on the shield. The second theory is perhaps the most popular, and speculates that the balls represent pills or glass jars used for bleeding, tools of doctors, the Italian word from which "medici" is derived. This theory may be incorrect though, as the associated tools of the medical practice may not pre-date the earliest versions of the crest. A more likely possibility is that the balls are derived from symbols on the crest for the Guild of Moneychangers (Arte del Cambio), the profession from which the Medicis made the bulk of their early wealth.

items.title: Cornelia, Mother of Gracchi
items.description:
A statue carved from Marble. The image depicts Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi brothers, along side her two sons. She stands with one arm supporting her baby son, and the other arm draped over the shoulder of the older. She is dressed in an elaborately draped dress and a shawl. Her hair is neatly groomed, pulled back into a tight bun with her bangs held back by a band.
The younger son, Gaius Gracchus, depicted here as a baby is supported on her left arm. He has his head laid on her shoulder, pillowed on his arm. His eyes are closed, as if peacefully asleep, and his other hand rests over her collar.
The older son, Tiberius Gracchus, is depicted about 10 years old, and stands at his mother's left hip. Both of the boys are nude, but while Gaius is covered by his positioning, Tiberius is covered by a fig leaf. He holds a scroll open in his hands and as if he is reading it. His hair is arranged in neat, shoulder length ringlets.

items.title: (1/2) Bronze relief after Donatello
items.description:
Bronze relief of a young angel. His body pushes forward from the frame, though his feet are planted behind the bottom of the frame. He is turned over his left shoulder, and the right wing peaks past the edge of the frame. He is blowing a trumpet, which is aimed up and back behind the frame in the direction that he is facing. He wears a tunic and is haloed with short hair.
This relief is a modern loose rendering of the same image by Donatello. The original bronzes are a set of 12 musical angels, which adorn the High Altar at the Basilica di Sant’Antonio, Padua. The originals are rendered in more detail than the recreations in LFC's collections. The originals are slightly larger, approximately 22.8"H x 8.3"W.

items.title: Lunette of Saint Anna, the Virgin and 2 Monks
items.description:
A Ceramic Lunette, which is rendered in 8 parts. The central image shows the Madonna and child. Behind Mary, with a hand on her shoulders is St. Anne; they are positioned to appear as if Mary is Sitting on Anne's lap with the infant Christ subsequently sitting in hers. Two Male saints kneel, one on each side, with their heads bowed toward the infant Christ. The three saints are haloed, thought the Virgin and Child are not, presumably because the are suspended too far forward in relief and would block the other figures. Around the top of the arch a Mask is presented at the crown of the arch, sculpted greenery and fruits then fall down either side of the arch.
Saint Anne is identified in her hagiography as the mother of the Virgin Mary. This explains her positioning with this pointedly young-looking depiction of the Virgin. Mary wears blue, so she stands out completely against the white glaze finish of her mother, the other two saints, and the Baby in her lap. The three older saints in turn stand out against the blue background, with Saint Anne acting as a sort of border around the Virgin.
The male saint on the right side of the image (when viewing) is St. Dominic. He holds a cross, Lilies and a book (there is also a scull nestled in the crook of his arm, though this is less typical of his attributes). He is dressed in robes and has his hair cut into a tonsure but is clean shaven.
The Second male saint, on the left side, is St. Augustine of Hippo. He holds a book against his knee. The symbol of a book is very common among saints, but is an attribute of Augustine. In his other hand he holds what appears to be a flaming heart, which would be a more identifiable symbols of Augustine.

items.title: Madonna with Angels
items.description:
A relief sculpture cast from paster. It depicts the Virgin Mary, standing straight backed and looking out over the viewer with a calm sort of serenity on her face. Supported on her right arm, the infant Christ is settled, looking in the same direction with a similar expression. He left hand holds his right over both of their hearts and his free hand loops over her shoulder to hold on. Surrounding them are five angels, all of whom are depicted young and appear looking on the Madonna and Child with open wonder on their faces.
The image is a (probably Modern) reproduction of a work originally carved from Marble. The original sculptor, Agostino di Duccio (1418 – c. 1481), was active in Prato alongside Donatello and Michelozzo. Both of the other artists' influence can be seen in his work. The Madonna with Angels was worked on between the years of 1463 and 1470. It is displayed in the Bargello in Florence, Italy. The recreation seems to be on the same scale.
